chapter.title: Two C libraries side by side: musl and glibc

section.title: Why two C libraries
section.para: Every dynamically linked program on Linux is bound to one C library: its ELF header names that library's dynamic loader, and its code calls that library's ABI. The two C libraries in wide use are not interchangeable:

listitem.para: The C library of most Linux distributions. Prebuilt software — commercial applications, games, vendor SDKs and drivers, many language runtimes and their binary packages — is published for glibc and does not run on musl.

section.para: On an FHS system both would compete for /lib, /lib64, /usr/include, the loader path, ldd and the compiler. DHS gives each its own directory and rules for which programs use which, so a distribution can be built on either C library and still run software built for the other, without either breaking the other.

listitem.para: The primary C library is the one the system layer is built against. Each distribution chooses it: musl or glibc. It always lives in the system layer.
The secondary C library is the other one. It is optional and lets the system run software built for it.

important.title: Where the secondary C library lives varies by distribution
important.para: A distribution decides whether it ships the secondary C library in the system layer (installed on every system, so base programs may use it) or offers it as a userland package (installed only when the user needs it). Both are conforming. In either case the secondary C library lives in its own triplet directory and follows the rules of ; only the layer differs. If the secondary C library is a userland package, the system layer MUST NOT contain files linked against it, and a base upgrade MUST reject such files, so that removing the package cannot break the base.

section.title: Design A: musl primary, glibc secondary
section.para: The base is built against musl. glibc is added for prebuilt glibc software.
section.programlisting: /overlayer/ ├── syshub/ │ ├── bin/ lib/ include/ … musl programs and libraries │ ├── arch-vendor-linux-musl/ primary │ │ ├── lib/ld-musl-arch.so.1 lib/libc.so │ │ ├── include/ │ │ └── bin/ musl toolchain (cross-named) │ └── arch-vendor-linux-gnu/ secondary, when shipped in the base └── userland/union/ └── arch-vendor-linux-gnu/ secondary, when offered as a package ├── lib/ld-linux-arch.so.2 lib/libc.so.6 lib/libstdc++.so.6 … ├── include/ ├── bin/ ldd, iconv, locale, gnu toolchain └── etc/ ld.so.conf, ld.so.cache

note.title: Implementation note
note.para: Zainium OS uses design A with glibc as a userland package (glibc, glibc-dev, glibc-toolchain) in /overlayer/zexlib/union/x86_64-zainium-linux-gnu; the base rejects files linked against glibc.

section.title: Design B: glibc primary, musl secondary
section.para: The base is built against glibc, as most distributions are today. musl is added for software built for musl distributions, or for building small static programs.
section.programlisting: /overlayer/ ├── syshub/ │ ├── bin/ lib/ include/ … glibc programs and libraries │ ├── arch-vendor-linux-gnu/ primary │ │ ├── lib/ld-linux-arch.so.2 lib/libc.so.6 … │ │ ├── include/ │ │ ├── bin/ ldd, iconv, locale, gnu toolchain │ │ └── etc/ ld.so.conf, ld.so.cache │ └── arch-vendor-linux-musl/ secondary, when shipped in the base └── userland/union/ └── arch-vendor-linux-musl/ secondary, when offered as a package ├── lib/ld-musl-arch.so.1 lib/libc.so ├── include/ ├── bin/ musl toolchain └── etc/ ld-musl-arch.path

glibc, in the system layer or as a userland package
musl, in the system layer or as a userland package

section.title: Directories
section.para: Each C library is installed into a directory named after its GNU target triplet: arch-vendor-linux-musl for musl, arch-vendor-linux-gnu for glibc. The primary one is in the system layer; the secondary one is in the system layer or in /overlayer/userland/union.

row.entry: lib/libc.so.6 and the other glibc libraries
libstdc++ and libgcc_s: the primary's copies in the shared lib, the secondary's in its own lib

section.title: The shared directories belong to the primary C library
section.para: The secondary C library MUST NOT install anything into the shared bin, sbin, lib or include of the system view. As a result cc, the headers in the default search path, ldd and every library in /overlayer/syshub/lib belong to the primary C library, and installing the secondary changes none of them.

section.title: Every program names its own loader
section.para: The ELF interpreter (PT_INTERP) of every dynamically linked program MUST be the DHS path of the loader of the C library it was linked against. A program therefore always starts with the right loader, whichever C libraries are installed.

section.title: Library search paths do not cross

listitem.para: The primary loader searches, in this order, /overlayer/syshub/lib, the primary triplet lib directory and /overlayer/userland/union/lib. Base programs SHOULD also carry /overlayer/syshub/lib as their library path (RPATH).

The secondary loader MUST search only its own lib directory and the directories named in its own configuration. It MUST NOT search /overlayer/syshub/lib: the libraries there are built for the primary C library and cannot be loaded into a process of the other.
Libraries that programs of the secondary C library need — including its C++ runtime — are installed into the secondary's lib directory.

section.title: Both C libraries read the same system configuration
section.para: Users, groups, passwords, host names, DNS and the time zone are system facts, not library facts. The paths compiled into every C library on the system MUST point at the system layer:

row.entry: /etc/passwd, group, shadow, hosts, resolv.conf, nsswitch.conf, localtime

section.para: A C library SHOULD be built with these paths changed by source patches, so that no symbolic links are needed.

listitem.para: The unprefixed compiler names (cc, gcc, g++, c99) MUST belong to the primary C library.

The secondary C library's compiler MUST be installed under its triplet name only, MUST take its headers, start files and libraries from the secondary's directory, and MUST write the secondary loader's DHS path into the programs it links.
Each toolchain has its own pkg-config search path, so that a build against one C library never picks up .pc files of the other.
An implementation MAY let the user select which toolchain the unprefixed names run, per shell or as a system setting. The default MUST be the primary C library.

note.title: Implementation note
note.para: On Zainium OS, sys-resolver env glibc prints the environment that makes cc, gcc, g++, cpp and pkg-config use glibc in the current shell; elevate sys-resolver set glibc|musl changes the system default and sys-resolver get shows it. The variable ZAINIUM_LIBC overrides the setting for one command.

section.title: Package managers keep each program on its own C library
section.para: A package manager that adapts foreign packages to DHS paths () MUST recognise which C library each program and library was linked against — by its interpreter or its dependency on libc.so.6 or libc.so — and MUST NOT rewrite its loader or library path to the other C library's.

row.entry: What goes wrong when both share FHS paths
Both loaders and both libc files compete for /lib and /lib64; a package of one library can overwrite the other's.
Each loader is in its own triplet directory; every program names its own ().
Compiling against one library's stdio.h and linking against the other's libc produces programs that fail at run time.
Each library's headers are in its own include; each compiler uses only its own.
A program of one library finds a library built for the other in /usr/lib and crashes or fails to load.
The secondary loader never searches the shared lib ().
libstdc++ and libgcc_s built for one library are loaded by programs of the other.
Each library has its own copies.
ldconfig lists libraries of both in one ld.so.cache.
Each loader's configuration lives in its own directory and lists only its own libraries.
The secondary's ldd or iconv replaces the primary's and gives wrong answers for base programs.
The secondary's tools stay in its own bin, off PATH.
A build picks up .pc files of the wrong library.
Two libraries read users, DNS or the time zone from different places and disagree.
Both read the system layer's etc ().
A program built on another distribution names /lib64/ld-linux-x86-64.so.2 or /lib/ld-musl-x86_64.so.1, which a DHS root does not have.
The missing loader path is redirected to the installed loader of the same C library ().
